meta.title: Door in the Face
meta.subtitle: A Field Guide to the Discount Trick and How to Stop It
meta.description: Twelve cards on the door-in-the-face technique — how it works, why it works on almost everyone, and how to spot it, stop it, and use it before they do.
meta.author: AI

generation.topic: Defending against the door-in-the-face discount trick

cards.title: Spot the Opening Offer That Was Never Real
cards.hook: The first price they name was built to be refused. The move starts before you say a word.
cards.truth:
The big ask is not a real position. It is furniture that makes the second ask look fair.
• The opener is designed to be refused. Its only job is to exist.
• After you say no, the second number feels like a win. It is not.
• The trap: you judge the second ask against the first, not against what the thing is actually worth.
cards.remember: The first offer is a prop, not a price.
cards.theySee: A seller naming a price so high the buyer laughs — then watching the buyer stay in the room.

signals.t: The opening number is far above any reasonable range — five times, ten times, more.
They drop their price almost immediately after you say no, without hesitation or calculation.
The follow-up number arrives without any pause — they had it prepared before you walked in.
They say 'I'll do it for X' as if they are personally doing you a favor.

steps.title: Write your number first
steps.desc: Before any conversation starts, write down what you think the item is actually worth. Do not change it until after the meeting ends.

steps.title: Let the opener die
steps.desc: Hear the big number, say nothing, let the silence sit. Do not react emotionally or visibly.

steps.title: Name your number as if theirs never happened
steps.desc: State your price directly. 'I'm thinking X.' Do not reference their opener at all.

cards.script: "Let's start from what it's actually worth. What's your floor?"
cards.counter:
The opener only works if you lose your own number before they say theirs.
• Notice if you can no longer remember what you thought it was worth before they spoke.
• Say 'What's the real price?' not 'What's the discount?'
• Write your number before any conversation starts and keep it.
cards.insight: The opener only works if you didn't do the math before you walked in. The harder question is whether you did.

cards.title: The Second Number Feels Cheap Because the First Was Absurd
cards.hook: You did not get a discount. You got a new reference point.
cards.truth:
Contrast replaces your price memory with their anchor.
• Standing next to a big number, a smaller number looks small — even if it is still too high.
• You compare the second ask to the first, not to what the thing is worth on the open market.
• The trap: you walk away feeling like a winner who paid twice the fair price.
cards.remember: Your brain judges prices against each other, not against real value.
cards.theySee: A buyer relaxing after hearing the lower number — because the higher one made it feel like relief.

signals.t: Your instinct rejected the opener immediately. That reaction was the setup for what came next.
Something relaxed in you when the second number landed, even before you checked if it was fair.
You stopped checking other sellers or prices after they came down on their ask.
You heard yourself say 'that's not bad, considering' without knowing what you were comparing it to.

steps.title: Look up the market price first
steps.desc: Before any price conversation, find the actual market rate for the item. Write it down. This is your only reference point.

steps.title: Compare to market, not to opener
steps.desc: When the second ask arrives, ask: is this fair against the market? Not: is this fair against what they first said?

steps.title: Say the market price out loud
steps.desc: Name your reference point before agreeing to anything. 'The market rate is around X. Can we work from there?'

cards.script: "That's better, but the market rate is around X. Can we work from there?"
cards.counter:
This move works on anyone who forgets to bring their own benchmark.
• Ask: 'What would I pay if I heard only the second number, never the first?'
• If the answer is 'less,' you are still inside their trap.
• Reset by naming the market rate before going any further.
cards.insight: The real damage is not the price you paid. It is that you stopped asking whether the second number was fair on its own.

cards.title: Their Concession Creates a Debt You Did Not Ask For
cards.hook: They dropped their price. You didn't ask them to. Now you feel a debt that isn't real.
cards.truth:
The norm of reciprocity fires even when the original ask was fake.
• They gave up nothing — the opener was always going to be refused.
• Your brain registers a concession and wants to balance the ledger.
• The trap: you agree to a bad deal because saying no twice feels ungrateful.
cards.remember: When someone gives ground, your brain says give something back.
cards.theySee: A person who already said no once, now nodding — because the seller came down for them.

signals.t: Declining the follow-up offer feels more difficult than declining the first one did.
They remind you they 'moved a lot' to get to this number, as if it cost them something real.
You apologize while declining the second ask, as if refusing is your fault.
You leave feeling like you treated them unfairly rather than like you held a position.

steps.title: Write this before you go in
steps.desc: Write: 'I owe them nothing for dropping a number they set too high.' Read it before you sit down.

steps.title: Acknowledge without moving
steps.desc: When they come down, say thank you and do not shift your position. Gratitude is not agreement.

steps.title: Let silence sit after their move
steps.desc: Do not fill the quiet after their concession with a yes. The discomfort is theirs to manage.

cards.script: "I appreciate you moving on that. I'm still at X."
cards.counter:
If their concession suddenly makes you want to agree, ask what actually changed.
• Ask: 'Did the value change, or just the number they're asking?'
• If only the number changed, the product is the same. Your obligation is zero.
• Say thank you and hold your number.
cards.insight: Reciprocity is a social rule built for real gifts. This technique borrows that rule and applies it to a gift that was never given.

cards.title: Fear of Looking Selfish Closes the Deal for Them
cards.hook: You already said no once. Saying no again feels like you're the problem. That feeling is the move.
cards.truth:
The fear of seeming unreasonable does more selling than any price drop.
• After refusing a big ask, people feel they have already refused enough for one conversation.
• The second ask offers a way to prove they are not cheap or difficult — to look fair again.
• The trap: you buy your reputation back with a bad deal.
cards.remember: You say yes to look fair, not because the deal was fair.
cards.theySee: A buyer looking uncomfortable after saying no — scanning the room for a way to stop feeling like the difficult one.

signals.t: You give detailed reasons for saying no instead of just saying it and stopping.
You say 'I wish I could' rather than 'I won't' — softening your own position.
You suggest a split nobody asked for, to ease your own discomfort after saying no.
After saying no, you check their expression for signs they are upset or disappointed.

steps.title: Accept that no twice is allowed
steps.desc: Before the meeting, decide that two refusals in a row is a normal thing to do. Write it down if you need to.

steps.title: Drop the reasons
steps.desc: Say 'That doesn't work for me' with no explanation attached. Reasons invite negotiation. Silence doesn't.

steps.title: Do not fill the pause after no
steps.desc: If they go quiet after your second refusal, stay quiet. One sentence. Then stop talking.

cards.counter:
If you feel like the bad guy after saying no, ask who put that feeling there.
• They built the opener to make your second no feel selfish. It was planned.
• You owe them nothing for refusing a fake price.
• One sentence, no explanation, hold the position.
cards.insight: The guilt is real. But it was installed deliberately. The harder question is what it would take for you to say no twice without feeling like you owe an apology.

cards.title: Name Your Price Before They Name Theirs
cards.hook: Whoever names a number first sets the gravity of the room. Let it be you.
cards.truth:
The side that anchors first makes the other side adjust — not the other way around.
• An early anchor makes every number after look like a step away from yours, not theirs.
• DITF only works if they anchor first. Take the anchor before they open their mouth.
• The trap: waiting to 'see what they say' hands them control before you say a word.
cards.remember: The first number said out loud controls the whole conversation.
cards.theySee: A buyer who speaks first — naming a specific number — before the seller has said anything about price.

signals.t: After you name your number, they go quiet and recalibrate before responding.
They have to explain why their number is higher than yours instead of simply stating it.
The conversation moves toward your number rather than away from it.
They skip the inflated opener entirely when your anchor is already on the table.

steps.title: Research the real market range
steps.desc: The night before, find the actual market floor and ceiling for what you're buying. Know both numbers before you walk in.

steps.title: Open with a specific number
steps.desc: In the first 60 seconds, name a number slightly below your real target. Specific beats round. '47' beats '50'.

steps.title: Hold the anchor when they push back
steps.desc: If they try to open above yours, say: 'I've done my homework. Let's start from X.'

cards.script: "Based on what I've seen in the market, I'm thinking X. Where are you?"
cards.counter:
If someone anchors before you can, don't accept their number as the starting point.
• Say 'Let me set a different starting point' and name yours.
• Never negotiate down from their number. Negotiate up from yours.
• The deal lands in the range between two anchors. Pick your end.
cards.insight: Going first feels risky. Going second means you spend the whole meeting adjusting toward someone else's number. Those are not equal risks.

cards.title: Name the Trick Out Loud and Watch It Stop Working
cards.hook: This move only works in the dark. Switch the light on.
cards.truth:
DITF depends on the target not knowing the mechanism. Name it and the mechanism breaks.
• When you say 'that's the big-first-ask move,' the concession loses its emotional weight.
• The guilt and reciprocity effects run below your awareness to work. Naming them shuts them down.
• The trap for them: once you name it, they cannot un-name it. The room has changed.
cards.remember: Say the name of the trick and it stops working.
cards.theySee: A buyer calmly saying the name of the technique while the seller realizes the move is visible.

signals.t: They come down within seconds of hearing your no — no hesitation, no calculation at all.
The difference between the opener and the second ask is more than 30 percent.
You hear them use the exact same big number with someone else in earshot.
Their concession cost them nothing visibly — they showed no hesitation giving it up.

steps.title: Check the gap
steps.desc: If the first ask and second ask are more than 30 percent apart and the drop came fast, you are looking at DITF.

steps.title: Say it out loud, calmly
steps.desc: Say: 'This looks like a big-first-ask move.' Calm voice. Not accusatory. Just naming what you see.

steps.title: Restate your number
steps.desc: After naming it, state your price as if the opener never happened. 'What's the real number you would take?'

cards.script: "That opener was too high to be real. What's the actual number you'd take?"
cards.counter:
If someone names YOUR move out loud, do not deny it.
• Denying it makes you look worse. Acknowledge it and move on.
• Say: 'Fair point. Here's where I actually am.'
• Credibility you get back is worth more than the concession you tried to extract.
cards.insight: Naming the move is its own power move — but only if you look calm doing it. Anger or smugness turns the room against you instead of them.

cards.title: Judge Every Offer on Its Own, Not Against the One Before It
cards.hook: The second ask sounds fair because you heard the first one. Forget the first one.
cards.truth:
Your brain uses the opener as a reference point. Wipe it deliberately.
• Ask: 'If the opener never happened, would I accept this number?' If no, nothing changed.
• The product hasn't changed between the first and second ask. Only the number has.
• The trap: calling a bad deal fair because a worse one came right before it.
cards.remember: Ask what you'd pay if you heard only this number.
cards.theySee: A buyer pausing and running their own internal check before responding to the new offer on the table.

signals.t: You feel good about the second ask just because it is lower than the first — not because it is fair.
You stopped looking at outside prices after they came down on their ask.
You are moving toward agreement before you have run the actual math on the deal.
You can no longer remember what you came in planning to pay.

steps.title: Pause before responding
steps.desc: When a new offer lands, do not respond immediately. Give yourself ten seconds to run the isolation check.

steps.title: Run the isolation test
steps.desc: Ask: 'What would I pay if the first number had never been said?' Compare that answer to the new ask.

steps.title: Compare to market, not to opener
steps.desc: If the new ask is above market, say so. 'I need to get closer to market on this.'

cards.script: "Forget the first number. This one still needs to come down to about X."
cards.counter:
If resetting feels socially awkward, that awkwardness is part of the move.
• Your real limit is the number you had before they spoke. Protect it.
• Practice by never reacting to a first offer. Pause. Then respond.
• People will call you difficult. That is the compliance mechanism talking.
cards.insight: The hardest version of this defense is using it on people you like. Social warmth is the technique's best cover.

cards.title: Delay the Decision Until the Contrast Fades
cards.hook: The second offer feels most reasonable right after the first is refused. Walk away for ten minutes.
cards.truth:
The contrast effect is time-limited. Waiting reduces its power significantly.
• The feeling that 'they came down for me' fades fast once you step away from the table.
• A buyer who waits loses the contrast feeling and gets their own reference point back.
• The trap: deciding in the room, under the full weight of the contrast, right when they want you to.
cards.remember: The contrast effect is strongest right after the first offer. Wait it out.
cards.theySee: A buyer saying 'let me think about that' and physically walking away from the table.

signals.t: They ask for a decision before you leave — urgency that wasn't there before.
A time limit gets added to the second ask that was not mentioned with the first.
They throw in something extra to keep you in the room and stop you leaving.
You want to decide fast because the deal feels good right now — that urgency is theirs, not yours.

steps.title: Say you need a few minutes
steps.desc: When the second offer lands, say: 'I want to think on that.' Do not give an answer while you are in the room.

steps.title: Physically leave
steps.desc: Walk out of the shop, step outside, go to a different room. The physical distance matters. Ten minutes minimum.

steps.title: Ask the clean question
steps.desc: After ten minutes: 'What is this worth without any of that conversation in my head?' That number is your real answer.

cards.script: "I want to think on that. I'll come back to you."
cards.counter:
If they add urgency to stop you leaving, the urgency is part of the same move.
• Real scarcity is real. Invented scarcity disappears when you walk away and come back.
• If the deal is real, it will be there in ten minutes.
• Never let a deadline they set override a number you calculated.
cards.insight: Most bad deals get signed in the first 90 seconds after a concession. The next question is what you do when you come back — after the contrast has faded and your own number is clear again.

cards.title: Open High First and Let Them Think They Won
cards.hook: You know they're going to open absurd. Get there first.
cards.truth:
If you anchor with an extreme ask before they do, their opener looks moderate — and they lose the contrast advantage.
• Open with a number you know they will refuse. Watch them scramble for a counter.
• When you drop to your real target, it looks like a concession they earned.
• The trap for them: they thought they had the playbook. You had it first.
cards.remember: Make the first extreme ask before they do.
cards.theySee: A buyer making an extremely low first offer — before the seller has said a single word about price.

signals.t: They react to your opener the way you usually react to theirs.
They explain why your number is too low — now anchoring against yours instead of the other way around.
They make the first real price movement because you set the tempo of the room.
They become more careful and less confident than they were when they walked in.

steps.title: Set your opening number the night before
steps.desc: Pick a number 30–40 percent below your real target. Write it down and commit to it before you sit down.

steps.title: Say it flat
steps.desc: State your opening number without apology, hesitation, or explanation. 'I'm at X.' Stop there.

steps.title: Drop to your real target as your concession
steps.desc: When they push back, move to your actual target. Frame it as you meeting them. 'I can work up to Y if you can move on Z.'

cards.script: "I was thinking more like X. But I can work up to Y if you can move on Z."
cards.counter:
Two people using DITF at each other produces a standoff, not a deal.
• If both sides anchored extreme, call it: 'We both opened big. What's your real floor?'
• The first one to show a real number gives a little. The first one to ask for it often gets it.
• Whoever calls the reset first usually controls what comes after it.
cards.insight: Using DITF first works once. Research shows the person who detects it will punish you in the next round. Know which game you are playing before you start.

cards.title: If They Detect the Move, They Will Punish You in Round Two
cards.hook: The technique worked. They bought. But they noticed. And they will remember.
cards.truth:
Research at Hang Seng and Harvard shows detected DITF makes the other side demand more next time and trust you less.
• Sellers who caught the move in round one made harder opening demands in round two.
• They also picked a different partner for follow-on work more often than those who did not detect it.
• The trap: you won one deal and lost the relationship — or every deal that follows it.
cards.remember: Getting caught using this trick costs you the next deal.
cards.theySee: A seller in a second meeting sitting down with a noticeably tougher position — and not explaining why.

signals.t: Their first number in the next meeting is higher than it was last time for no clear reason.
The small talk before business is shorter or gone entirely compared to before.
They introduce terms and conditions they never mentioned in any previous conversation.
They say they are talking to a few others — something they did not say before.

steps.title: Assess detection risk after every deal
steps.desc: Ask yourself: could they see the big-then-small pattern? If yes, plan a different opening for next time.

steps.title: Open the next meeting with your real number
steps.desc: If they likely detected it, skip the opener entirely. Name your real position in the first sentence.

steps.title: Name it if the relationship matters
steps.desc: Say: 'Last time I opened high. Here's where I actually am this time.' That one sentence buys back more trust than the opener ever earned.

cards.script: "I want to start clean this time. Here's my real number upfront."
cards.counter:
If someone's second-round demands are harder for no clear reason, suspect detected manipulation from last time.
• Ask yourself: did you use a big-then-small sequence they could have spotted?
• If yes, skip the opener and go straight to your real position this time.
• Relationships built on repeated manipulation need constant escalation. That math stops working fast.
cards.insight: The reciprocity norm works both ways. Give them a fake opener and they will give you one back — bigger than yours was — and feel completely justified doing it.

cards.title: Spot DITF in Retail Pricing and Abandoned Cart Emails
cards.hook: The crossed-out price in red is doing the same thing as the flea market vendor. The algorithm learned it too.
cards.truth:
Retailers build DITF into their pricing architecture so no human has to run the move live.
• A $500 crossed-out price next to $100 runs the same contrast trick as the antique clock story in the source.
• Abandoned cart emails that send a discount code run the same sequence: big price shown, you leave, smaller price arrives.
• The trap: the 'original' price was never a real transaction. It is furniture, same as the absurd opener.
cards.remember: Retail pricing runs the same trick without a human seller.
cards.theySee: A shopper looking at a crossed-out price and a sale number — feeling like they caught the store on a good day.

signals.t: A higher number is struck through next to the current price — displayed as if it was ever real.
An email arrives within minutes of you closing a browser tab, offering a discount code.
A large free-shipping threshold is set, then a lower one or a code appears when you start to leave.
A sale activates right when you hesitate on the full price, as if triggered by your behavior.

steps.title: Check the actual market price
steps.desc: Before buying anything online, search the item on a comparison site. The crossed-out number tells you nothing.

steps.title: Ignore the crossed-out number entirely
steps.desc: Judge the current price against the market. The original price is not a reference point. It is a prop.

steps.title: Wait for the cart email
steps.desc: Leave the cart. If a discount code arrives, you have found the real floor. Buy at that price or keep waiting.

cards.counter:
Retailers count on you never checking whether the original price reflected actual past transactions.
• Tools like CamelCamelCamel track Amazon price history over time. Check before you buy.
• If a discount appears right when you leave, the full price was always negotiable.
• The cart email is the second ask. The full price page was the first. You are in a DITF sequence.
cards.insight: The retail version is more dangerous than the human version because it runs at scale and never feels personal. Nobody is watching you — so you cannot call it out in the room.

cards.title: Know When the Deal Is Not Worth What the Move Costs You
cards.hook: DITF wins a price. It can lose a partner. Know which one you need more.
cards.truth:
The value of a price win shrinks fast against the cost of damaged trust with someone you will deal with again.
• Cialdini's 1975 study used strangers. Most real negotiations happen with people you will see again.
• A seller who detects the move becomes a harder counterpart in every deal that follows.
• The trap: treating a repeat relationship like a one-time sale.
cards.remember: A price win today can cost you the next deal.
cards.theySee: A regular supplier looking across a table at a buyer who just used a move they have seen before.

signals.t: This person is a vendor, colleague, or partner you see on a regular schedule.
They know other people in your field or market and talk to them.
Your market is small enough that what you do in one room reaches others.
Their previous asks have been reasonable — this is not a combative opener from a habitual DITF user.

steps.title: Decide before you negotiate
steps.desc: Write down: will I deal with this person again? If yes, the technique is likely too expensive. Choose a different approach.

steps.title: Start with your real number
steps.desc: With repeat contacts, open with your actual position and explain your reasoning briefly. It builds more over time than a single win does.

steps.title: If you're on the receiving end, say so
steps.desc: Tell them: 'I've seen this pattern before. Can we skip to real numbers?' One sentence. The relationship stays intact.

cards.script: "Here's where I actually need to land on this. Can we make that work?"
cards.counter:
If a long-term partner is using DITF on you, address it directly instead of playing along and resenting them.
• Say: 'I've seen this move before. Can we go straight to real numbers?'
• Playing along and resenting them later costs more than saying it once.
• One sentence protects the relationship more than any counter-tactic will.
cards.insight: The question is not whether DITF works — it does. The question is whether the price you need to win is lower than the price you will pay to win it.
